chunks: "For a typical LiPo or Li-ion cell the safe, standard charge rate is 0. 5C to 1C, so for a 2 amp-hour cell, 1 to 2 amps.
Plenty of manufacturers rate their cells for more, 2C or even higher for fast-charge or high-power cells, but the rule is that the datasheet number is the limit and I don't exceed it.
Why isn't it unlimited? The main danger is lithium plating.
If I push current faster than lithium can diffuse into the graphite, the surface potential of the anode drops below zero versus lithium and metal plates out.
That's permanent loss of capacity and can grow dendrites. It gets worse in the cold and at high state of charge, so the safe rate depends on conditions.
The other limit is heat: I to the 2R grows with the square of the current, so at 4C the cell heats sixteen times more than at 1C. There's also a diminishing return.
In my model, going from 1C to 2C only cuts the total charge time from 77 to 54 minutes, because the constant-voltage tail doesn't get shorter. So the extra stress buys little.

5 to 1C, only between about 0 and 45 degrees with reduced current near the cold end, with the charger terminating by current and a timer, and I'd use the faster rate only if the cell is specifically specified for it."
